titre: “Rain follows the plow”: a theory born of a few wet years
accroche: In 1881, Wilber claims that farming the Plains makes it rain. He has the correlation on his side, for a few years.
contenu_vulgarise:
The idea sounds like farmers' common sense: the more you cultivate, the more it rains. It had supporters in the American Great Plains, including an author who wrote a book about it.

## An unwelcome report

In 1878, John Wesley Powell, explorer and geologist, published a report on the arid lands of the West, reprinted in 1879. In it he set at 20 inches of rain a year, about 510 mm, the limit for farming without irrigation. The region that stays below that line corresponds roughly to the area west of the 100th meridian. Farming those lands requires irrigation, and therefore a different division of the land than the 160-acre plots provided by the 1862 settlement law, the Homestead Act.

The message was awkward for those with land to sell. The railroad companies, which had received land from the government, wanted to sell it at farmland prices.

## A reply that does not deny aridity

Charles Dana Wilber (1830-1891) answered in a book published in Omaha in 1881. He does not dispute that the West is drier than the East. He makes three points: rainfall increases, in multi-year periods, as you move west from the Missouri; this increase follows that of cultivation; and the relation is one of cause and effect. Hence the slogan.

The theory's supporters looked for a mechanism, and proposed several: turned-over soil would release its moisture, planted trees, train smoke, and even the metal of the rails would make it rain. The theory is now considered false.

## What correlation does not say

Wilber published during a relatively wet period. The fields advanced, and so did the rain, and he made the second a consequence of the first. The rainfall observations he cites may well have been real; the cause he gave them did not survive the drought that followed.

When the next dry cycle arrived, in the 1890s, the theory looked less plausible and, according to the historian who introduces the text, Powell's account more accurate. Powell testified on January 17, 1890 before a Senate committee, with a map in hand. According to Wikipedia, later rainfall records showed that the theory rested on brief climate fluctuations that happened to coincide with settlement.

## The shift

Two curves rise together for a few years: Wilber's argument rests on that coincidence alone, read as a cause, over a period too short to tell a climate from a fluctuation. That it suited those who sold land says nothing about whether it was true. It does explain, however, why it was believed without being tested.

The same question arises whenever a trend of a few years is used to establish a rule: over what period was it measured?

citation.texte: The relation here stated is that of cause and effect. In other words, rain follows the plow.
citation.source: The Great Valleys and Prairies of Nebraska and the Northwest, Omaha, Daily Republican Print, 1881, pp. 138-143

carte.punch: “Rain follows the plow”: in 1881, a theory born of a wet period.
carte.idee: Wilber (1881) argues that farming the American West makes it rain there: fields and rain were advancing together. But he was publishing during a wet period. When the dry spell returns, in the 1890s, the theory no longer holds.

quiz.question: Why did Wilber's theory lose its credibility in the 1890s?
choix: Because the railroads stopped supporting it and stopped selling land
Because Powell showed that the 100th meridian marked off no dry zone
Because a new dry cycle arrived, even as cultivation kept advancing
Because settlers had never measured any increase in rainfall in the 1870s
quiz.explication: The theory rested on a wet period. When the dry cycle returned in the 1890s, rainfall fell while cultivation was still advancing: the supposed cause no longer explained anything. The railroads had an interest in backing it as long as they were selling land, but that is not what ruined it; Powell defended aridity without disputing the observed increase; and that increase was real, it was its interpretation that did not hold.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What does Powell's report, published in 1878 and reprinted in 1879, set?
choix: The definitive boundary between the Great Plains and the Rockies
The exact number of settlers needed to populate the American West
The list of railroad companies authorized to sell public land
The limit of 20 inches of rain a year below which farming requires irrigation
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Powell sets at 20 inches, about 510 mm of annual rainfall, the limit below which farming requires irrigation.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What mechanisms did supporters of the “rain follows the plow” theory propose to explain it?
choix: Systematic crop rotation and repeated use of natural fertilizers on the same plots
Wind blowing from the Pacific Ocean all the way to the interior Great Plains
Soil turned over by the plow, planted trees, train smoke, the metal of the rails
The systematic construction of irrigation canals fully funded by the federal government
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Supporters put forward several mechanisms: turned-over soil releasing its moisture, trees, train smoke, the metal of the rails.

quiz_supplementaire.question: Why does Powell's report trouble the railroad companies?
choix: Because it flatly forbids them from owning any land in the American West
Because it implies a different division of land than 160-acre plots, for land they wanted to sell at farmland prices
Because it blames the smoke of the trains they operated for causing local drought
Because it demands the immediate nationalization of the country's entire railroad network
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The report implies a different division than the 160-acre plots of the Homestead Act, for land they wanted to sell at farmland prices.
